title: Pay for the work you actually need
lead: Tie optimization to a business requirement and a measured bottleneck.

sections.title: Understand the idea
sections.body: Persistent clusters may fit steady workloads; job-based compute may fit intermittent processing. Query scan reduction matters for on-demand analysis, while capacity-based execution requires attention to slots and utilization.

sections.title: Make the decision
sections.body: Reuse supported aggregates, stop idle compute, and compare storage, processing and network effects. A cheaper worker can cost more overall if it repeatedly fails or extends the job.

sections.title: Work through a scenario
sections.body: A weekly Spark job runs for thirty minutes. Keep durable input in object storage and compare an ephemeral cluster or serverless execution against a cluster left running all week.

sections.title: Measure total work and idle time
sections.body: Compare steady workloads with intermittent jobs. Keep input data durable while evaluating temporary compute. Account for storage, networking, processing, failed attempts and operating effort; a cheaper instance is not necessarily cheaper per successful business run. Use a representative completion target for every comparison.

sections.title: Distinguish price models from optimization
sections.body: On-demand analytical charges emphasize data processed; capacity models emphasize provisioned or consumed compute behavior. Reducing scanned bytes is still useful work reduction, but it does not guarantee an identical percentage reduction in a capacity bill. Review the actual model before interpreting a tuning result.

sections.title: Use feedback to protect the business objective
sections.body: Measure run duration, freshness, failures and resource utilization before and after a change. A cost optimization that violates the required completion time is not a complete solution. Keep the comparison’s input volume and business logic fixed, and identify any changed reliability or operational assumptions.

trap: Reducing machine size is not an optimization if it violates the completion deadline.

exercise.prompt: A team reduces scan volume by 90% and promises a 90% reduction in its capacity-based bill. Is that conclusion supported?
exercise.answer: Not by scan volume alone. It shows less logical read work under the measured query, but the bill depends on the capacity configuration, utilization and other charges. Compare actual usage under the billing model while checking that the output and deadline remain correct.
checkpoints: Compare cost per successful business result.
Distinguish on-demand and capacity considerations.
Keep the workload fixed during a tuning comparison.

review.scope: Retained original lesson and prior editorial references. Only claims listed in the current verification ledger were rechecked in this update.

briefing.context: A Spark job runs once a week while its cluster can remain allocated all week.
briefing.whyItMatters: Idle resources can consume budget without improving the required business outcome.
briefing.takeaway: Compare resource lifetime with the work that actually needs it.

title: Control query cost with the correct pricing model
lead: Bytes scanned, slot capacity and result row count answer different questions.

sections.title: Choose the cost signal
sections.body: For on-demand BigQuery queries, use a dry run as an estimate and configure maximum bytes billed where appropriate. A LIMIT on a non-clustered table does not reduce the bytes read. Selecting fewer required columns and filtering partitions address the scan rather than just truncating the result.

sections.title: Separate capacity from scans
sections.body: Capacity-based workloads use slot capacity and reservations. Reduce wasted work, but also inspect concurrency, queuing and slot contention. A faster query and a smaller bill are related only through the applicable pricing and capacity contract.

sections.title: Compare an original workload
sections.body: A report scans the same historical columns for many consumers. Test a narrower projection, partition pruning and a suitable reusable result. Compare bytes, runtime, freshness and concurrent behavior before adopting the change. Keep illustrative scan models separate from a real invoice estimate.

trap: LIMIT 10 is a result-size control, not a universal query-cost ceiling.

exercise.prompt: A dashboard adds LIMIT 100 to SELECT * on a non-clustered table. What should the engineer inspect next?
exercise.answer: Inspect projected columns, partition filters and estimated bytes, then the execution evidence. Set an appropriate query guardrail for on-demand use and evaluate capacity behavior separately.
checkpoints: Identify the pricing model.
Separate result rows from scanned bytes.
Measure freshness as well as runtime.

review.scope: The specific service claims in this original lesson were checked against its primary references; the scenario is illustrative.

decision.advantage: Cost controls can prevent an unexpectedly large scan before it runs.
decision.limitation: An estimate or a local scan model is not a production bill.
decision.useCase: Reduce repeated dashboard work while preserving the required freshness.

briefing.context: A dashboard adds LIMIT 10 and expects a much smaller query bill.
briefing.whyItMatters: On a non-clustered BigQuery table, fewer returned rows do not mean fewer bytes read.
briefing.takeaway: Separate result size, scan work and the applicable pricing model.
briefing.scope: Original learning scenario and short-session guidance; primary references belong to the full lesson.

title: Make every retry intentional
lead: A directed acyclic graph makes task dependencies visible.

sections.title: Understand the idea
sections.body: Composer uses Airflow DAGs for scheduled workflows with task dependencies. Workflows coordinates service calls without managing an Airflow environment. An idempotent task supports safer retries and partial reruns.

sections.title: Make the decision
sections.body: Use separate tasks when separate failure recovery matters. Pass a stable run identifier, make writes repeatable, and define completion and failure alerts.

sections.title: Work through a scenario
sections.body: A daily process fetches files, decrypts them and runs SQL. Separate DAG tasks allow rerunning only the failed stage while preserving evidence of successful earlier stages.

sections.title: Make run identity explicit
sections.body: A task should know the logical input interval or batch it is processing. A retry, delayed execution or historical backfill should not silently switch to whatever the wall clock calls today. Use that logical interval to choose inputs and output keys, and record the code or configuration version used.

sections.title: Choose boundaries that support recovery
sections.body: Separate fetch, decryption, staging, transformation and validation when they need independent retries. Make each task’s effects repeatable or transactional where possible. A task should succeed only after its expected output is usable; catching every error and reporting success defeats downstream dependency logic.

sections.title: A quality check must gate the consumer
sections.body: An assertion existing in a repository does not automatically mean every downstream action waits for it. Declare and test the appropriate assertion dependencies. Run a known failing input and verify that the curated consumer is blocked, rather than checking only that the assertion produced a red status somewhere.

trap: Putting the entire process inside one operator hides the recovery boundaries.
code:
# Illustrative DAG dependencies, not a full deployable DAG.
fetch_files >> decrypt_files >> load_staging >> transform_sql >> validate

exercise.prompt: A backfill for last month queries CURRENT_DATE and appends into today’s target. What should change?
exercise.answer: Parameterize the logical interval and define a repeatable write strategy for that interval. Use stable keys or replacement boundaries and gate publication on quality checks. Test the same interval twice and confirm that the resulting business total does not double.
checkpoints: Use logical intervals for retries and backfills.
Make task effects repeatable.
Prove that failed quality checks block publication.

review.scope: Retained original lesson and prior editorial references. Only claims listed in the current verification ledger were rechecked in this update.

briefing.context: An orchestrated workflow fails after one task has already written durable output.
briefing.whyItMatters: Retrying every step blindly can append duplicates or publish mixed intervals.
briefing.takeaway: Make repeated execution produce the intended state.

title: Make orchestration safe to retry
lead: A schedule coordinates tasks; deterministic inputs and controlled side effects make retries safe.

sections.title: Separate orchestration and execution
sections.body: Cloud Composer terminology appears in the exam guide; current documentation uses Managed Airflow. DAGs describe tasks and their dependencies. Let specialized services perform the large transformation while the orchestration layer starts, observes and coordinates the work.

sections.title: Pin the logical input
sections.body: Airflow recommends repeatable task effects and reading a specific data partition. A retry that reads latest data can see different inputs. Use the intended interval and stable outputs, then make publication depend on validation. Avoid passing required durable data through a worker-local file.

sections.title: Rehearse a partial failure
sections.body: Original scenario: a daily load succeeds but its notification task fails. Re-running should not append the same business rows again. Record the interval and operation identity, use an appropriate idempotent write pattern and test the failure after each durable side effect.

trap: A green DAG does not prove the produced data satisfies the business contract.

exercise.prompt: A retried task uses the current clock to choose its input folder. What changes?
exercise.answer: A later retry can read a different interval. Pin the logical input and output and verify idempotent effects, including downstream publication.
checkpoints: Pin the data interval.
Identify every durable side effect.
Block publication on quality.

review.scope: The specific service claims in this original lesson were checked against its primary references; the scenario is illustrative.

decision.advantage: Explicit dependencies make recovery and ownership easier to reason about.
decision.limitation: Orchestrator success does not validate data correctness automatically.
decision.useCase: Recover a failed daily pipeline without publishing duplicate business rows.

briefing.context: A daily load succeeds, then its notification fails and the workflow retries.
briefing.whyItMatters: Using the current clock or blindly appending can change the input or duplicate the output.
briefing.takeaway: Pin the logical interval and make durable side effects safe to repeat.
briefing.scope: Original learning scenario and short-session guidance; primary references belong to the full lesson.

title: Keep competing workloads from interfering
lead: Priority and capacity allocation are different controls.

sections.title: Understand the idea
sections.body: BigQuery reservations assign compute capacity to workloads. Baseline capacity and autoscaling affect resource availability and spend. Separate reservations can isolate dashboard work from heavy transformation jobs.

sections.title: Make the decision
sections.body: Measure usage before sizing capacity. Choose interactive or batch execution according to latency tolerance, and use reservation assignments for the intended projects or workloads.

sections.title: Work through a scenario
sections.body: Dashboards slow down during ETL. Assign them a deliberate capacity pool and place cost-sensitive ETL in another allocation rather than assuming an interactive label reserves resources.

sections.title: Separate resource isolation from job priority
sections.body: Interactive and batch priority describe execution behavior; reservation assignments allocate workload capacity. A latency-sensitive team can still compete for a shared pool if it has no deliberate resource boundary. Use measurements to choose assignments and capacity rather than assuming a priority label guarantees a dedicated allocation.

sections.title: Reason about baseline and elasticity
sections.body: Baseline capacity supplies a configured starting allocation. Autoscaling can add capacity according to the supported configuration and workload. The maximum is a capacity setting, not a complete fixed-spend guarantee across storage and other services. Inspect edition, assignment, idle sharing and usage behavior under the chosen configuration.

sections.title: Read billing controls literally
sections.body: A budget alert reports spend or triggers notification handling; it is not inherently a hard cap. Query-specific controls and resource quotas solve narrower problems. Protect business-critical execution while designing cost controls, and avoid shutting down essential processing as an unexamined side effect of a generic spending rule.

trap: A budget alert reports spend; it is not a guaranteed automatic spending cap.

exercise.prompt: Dashboards have an interactive priority label but still slow down during ETL. What design dimension has probably not been isolated?
exercise.answer: Inspect the capacity pool and reservation assignments. Job priority alone does not establish separate compute for dashboards. Use actual slot usage and contention evidence to decide whether isolation or a query-level optimization is required.
checkpoints: Distinguish capacity assignments from priority.
Explain baseline and autoscaling without a fixed-bill promise.
State what a budget alert does.

review.scope: Retained original lesson and prior editorial references. Only claims listed in the current verification ledger were rechecked in this update.

briefing.context: Scheduled reports and interactive analysts compete for analytical resources.
briefing.whyItMatters: A workload can miss its deadline because it waits for shared capacity, even with valid SQL.
briefing.takeaway: Inspect concurrency and allocate capacity against business priorities.

title: Diagnose the failure before scaling
lead: The exact error and execution stage matter more than a generic label.

sections.title: Understand the idea
sections.body: Observe freshness, lag, failed rows, task retries and resource utilization. BigQuery execution details and job metadata help distinguish slow scans, slot pressure, shuffle problems and memory-heavy operations.

sections.title: Make the decision
sections.body: Inspect the query plan and the full error message before changing capacity. Separate API request quotas from execution memory and compute availability.

sections.title: Work through a scenario
sections.body: A query fails during a large sort. Check the execution graph and memory pressure; reduce the sorted intermediate data or restructure the query rather than raising an unrelated API quota.

sections.title: Observe the business and the engine
sections.body: Track data freshness, completeness and rejected-record backlog alongside CPU, memory and job status. A pipeline can be technically running while the expected data never reaches its consumer. Define an actionable threshold, an owner and a runbook for the failure condition you intend to detect.

sections.title: Use the right evidence for the question
sections.body: Audit logs answer who performed relevant operations. Job metadata and execution details help explain query work and failure. Resource metrics describe saturation or backlog. Correlate these signals with a run identifier and logical interval instead of treating an isolated chart as proof of a root cause.

sections.title: Prefer a causal test over a generic fix
sections.body: If a stage is serial because of a hot key, adding workers may leave that stage unchanged. If a query creates a large intermediate join, increasing an unrelated API quota will not repair its grain. Form a specific hypothesis, make a controlled change and compare outputs and resource behavior under the same input.

trap: More slots do not guarantee that every Resources exceeded error disappears.

exercise.prompt: Worker CPU is moderate but event lag keeps rising and one key dominates a stage. What would you investigate?
exercise.answer: Inspect key distribution, per-stage parallelism and any serial work or downstream limit. More workers may not split work for a single key. Verify the hypothesis with stage-level evidence and a correctness-preserving redesign rather than scaling blindly.
checkpoints: Include freshness and data quality in monitoring.
Choose logs versus job metadata for a concrete question.
Test a specific bottleneck hypothesis.

review.scope: Retained original lesson and prior editorial references. Only claims listed in the current verification ledger were rechecked in this update.

briefing.context: A data job is late and the team sees several symptoms at once.
briefing.whyItMatters: Treating the most visible metric as the cause can waste time and money.
briefing.takeaway: Use source, stage and sink evidence to test a specific diagnosis.

title: Diagnose a query from its execution evidence
lead: A failure message is the beginning of a causal investigation.

sections.title: Separate queueing from expensive computation
sections.body: A query may wait for resources, scan excessive data, create a large join intermediate, sort too many rows or spend time handling skew. Job metadata and the execution graph help identify which stage matters. Compare the same input and query semantics when testing an improvement.

sections.title: Inspect the reason behind the error
sections.body: Resources exceeded can indicate different memory, shuffle or planning problems. API request rate quotas are a different constraint from execution memory. A capacity reservation can be appropriate for some workload issues, but is not a universal repair for every failing operator or excessively complex query plan.

sections.title: Use billing evidence correctly
sections.body: A dry run can estimate relevant processed bytes for supported queries. Actual clustered block pruning and runtime compute behavior have additional considerations. Query limits, job controls and budgets solve different problems. Record the billing model and the measured unit before translating a performance result into a cost claim.

trap: The first visible red chart is not necessarily the root cause.

exercise.prompt: A query fails in a large global sort. What evidence would distinguish a SQL redesign from buying more capacity?
exercise.answer: Inspect the error details and execution stage, including intermediate size and memory pressure. Test reducing the sort input or using an appropriate query structure under the same business result. Capacity information helps, but the failing operation still needs a specific diagnosis.
checkpoints: Separate queue time from computation.
Map an error to the right resource.
Interpret bytes and slots under the chosen billing model.

review.scope: Retained original lesson and prior editorial references. Only claims listed in the current verification ledger were rechecked in this update.

briefing.context: An analytical query becomes slow after the dataset or workload changes.
briefing.whyItMatters: Changing SQL at random can hide the bottleneck without fixing it.
briefing.takeaway: Use execution evidence to distinguish scan, join and resource contention problems.

title: Diagnose freshness across a streaming pipeline
lead: Trace where data waits before adding compute or suppressing an alert.

sections.title: Distinguish the observations
sections.body: Dataflow exposes freshness, system latency, throughput and backlog metrics. System latency measures time an element spends processing or waiting, subject to source visibility. Pub/Sub oldest unacknowledged age describes waiting subscription messages. These observations are related but not interchangeable.

sections.title: Follow the bottleneck
sections.body: Original incident: input traffic is steady, destination writes start failing, and upstream backlog grows while worker CPU stays modest. Inspect write errors, permissions, quota and destination capacity. Adding workers cannot repair a denied sink. Correlate stage evidence rather than diagnosing from CPU alone.

sections.title: Define an actionable outcome
sections.body: Illustrative SLO: curated orders should be queryable within five minutes for the agreed population. Specify the timestamp, denominator, observation point and late-event policy. Couple an alert to an owner, a bounded recovery action and a check that reconciles missing records after recovery.

trap: A healthy transport graph does not prove that the business dataset is complete.

exercise.prompt: Backlog rises while sink writes fail with permission errors. Is increasing worker count a sufficient fix?
exercise.answer: No. Repair the identity or permission path, then observe whether the backlog drains and reconcile delayed or failed outputs. Verify the diagnosis from logs and metrics.
checkpoints: Name the observation point and unit.
Correlate source, stage and sink evidence.
Reconcile data after recovery.

decision.advantage: Stage-specific evidence narrows the corrective action.
decision.limitation: Freshness metrics alone do not establish semantic completeness.
decision.useCase: Triage delayed analytics with source, processor and sink evidence.

briefing.context: Orders arrive on time, but the analytical dataset is late while sink writes fail.
briefing.whyItMatters: More workers cannot repair a denied write, and a CPU chart does not establish data freshness.
briefing.takeaway: Correlate source, stage and sink evidence before changing capacity.

title: Design recovery against explicit objectives
lead: State how much data may be lost and how quickly service must return.

sections.title: Understand the idea
sections.body: RPO limits tolerable data loss; RTO limits recovery time. BigQuery time travel, snapshots and cross-region replication address different failure and retention needs. A multi-region label alone is not a complete disaster recovery plan.

sections.title: Make the decision
sections.body: Match backup frequency and replication behavior to the objectives, then rehearse a restore. Check retention, permissions and the region of the recovery copy.

sections.title: Work through a scenario
sections.body: A daily export can leave nearly a day of changes unavailable, plus scheduling or export delays. A strict target below twenty-four hours needs an appropriate safety margin or a different replication approach.

sections.title: Specify the failure you are recovering from
sections.body: Accidental deletion, corrupted data, a zonal outage and regional unavailability are different events. A high-availability replica can preserve service during some infrastructure failures while also replicating a bad write. A backup retained in the same failed region may not satisfy regional recovery requirements.

sections.title: Measure the age of recoverable state
sections.body: RPO concerns the data state you can recover, not merely when a backup task started or finished. Include snapshot intervals, completion delays, replication lag and missed jobs in the loss model. RTO also includes detection, permissions, restoration, validation and consumer redirection. A table copy existing is not a rehearsed recovery procedure.

sections.title: Choose historical retention and disaster recovery separately
sections.body: Time travel can retrieve supported historical table states within its configured window. A retained snapshot can preserve a chosen state longer. Cross-region replication addresses a different failure domain and has its own supported capabilities. Verify locations, permissions and recovery operations against the actual incident requirement.

trap: Thirty-day backup retention and a thirty-day RPO describe different requirements.

exercise.prompt: A snapshot captured at 10:00 completes at 10:04. A failure at 10:03 leaves only the 09:30 snapshot complete. Which state is known recoverable?
exercise.answer: Under those stated assumptions, the latest completed recovery copy captures 09:30, so the potential data-loss interval at 10:03 is 33 minutes. Do not use the incomplete 10:00 copy or confuse completion delay with the age of recoverable data.
checkpoints: State the incident failure domain.
Compute data-loss age from recoverable state.
Separate historical retention, availability and regional recovery.

briefing.context: A dataset is corrupted or becomes unavailable during business hours.
briefing.whyItMatters: A backup exists only as a useful recovery option if it can meet the required data-loss and time objectives.
briefing.takeaway: State the failure, recovery point and recovery time you need to prove.
briefing.scope: Original learning scenario and short-session guidance; primary references belong to the full lesson.

title: Prove the recovery plan with a runbook
lead: A protected copy is useful only when the service can actually be restored.

sections.title: Write a failure-specific sequence
sections.body: State the incident scope, detection signal, person or automation making the decision, recovery source, required permissions and target. Include restoration, validation, connection or consumer redirection and the condition for declaring success. Do not count a backup filename as a tested runbook.

sections.title: Measure loss and restoration separately
sections.body: The age of the latest recoverable data state determines the potential RPO exposure under a given failure. RTO includes the time to detect and execute recovery, validate data and resume the business path. A fast copy operation does not prove a short end-to-end restoration objective.

sections.title: Rehearse with representative constraints
sections.body: A test should demonstrate the intended failure domain without corrupting production. Validate data totals, access, key availability and downstream behavior in the recovery environment. Record which assumptions were simulated, which were observed and what remains untested.

trap: Replication can reproduce a bad application write; availability does not replace historical recovery.

exercise.prompt: The backup restores successfully but the application account cannot read it. Has RTO been met?
exercise.answer: No, if the business service has not resumed. Access and consumer validation belong in the measured recovery procedure. Review the required roles, key permissions and redirection steps before declaring restoration complete.
checkpoints: Define the incident scope.
Measure recoverable-state age.
Include consumers and permissions in recovery evidence.

briefing.whyItMatters: An untested sequence can restore the wrong state or leave readers using incomplete data.
briefing.takeaway: Rehearse the restore and validate the recovered dataset before reopening it.
